claim: CIB2 and CIB3 bind to TMC1 and TMC2, the pore-forming subunits of the inner-ear mechano-electrical transduction (MET) apparatus.
source: Calcium and integrin-binding protein 2 (CIB2) and CIB3 bind to transmembrane channel-like 1 (TMC1) and TMC2, the pore-forming subunits of the inner-ear mechano-electrical transduction (MET) apparatus.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior work and is validated by experimental data presented in the manuscript including co-immunoprecipitation, NMR spectroscopy, and AlphaFold modeling.

claim: CIB2 and CIB3 can form heteromeric complexes with TMC1 and TMC2.
source: Here, we show that both CIB2 and CIB3 can form heteromeric complexes with TMC1 and TMC2 and are integral for MET function in mouse cochlea and vestibular end organs as well as in zebrafish inner ear and lateral line.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including biochemical assays, structural modeling, and functional studies in mouse and zebrafish presented in the manuscript.

claim: CIB2 and CIB3 are integral for MET function in mouse cochlea and vestibular end organs.
source: Here, we show that both CIB2 and CIB3 can form heteromeric complexes with TMC1 and TMC2 and are integral for MET function in mouse cochlea and vestibular end organs as well as in zebrafish inner ear and lateral line.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays including FM 1-43 dye uptake, ABR measurements, and vestibular function tests in Cib2/Cib3 knockout mice.

claim: CIB2 and CIB3 are integral for MET function in zebrafish inner ear and lateral line.
source: Here, we show that both CIB2 and CIB3 can form heteromeric complexes with TMC1 and TMC2 and are integral for MET function in mouse cochlea and vestibular end organs as well as in zebrafish inner ear and lateral line.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays including FM 1-43 dye uptake, acoustic startle response tests, and calcium imaging in zebrafish cib2 and cib3 mutants.

claim: Vertebrate CIB proteins can simultaneously interact with at least two cytoplasmic domains of TMC1 and TMC2.
source: Our AlphaFold 2 models suggest that vertebrate CIB proteins can simultaneously interact with at least two cytoplasmic domains of TMC1 and TMC2 as validated using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy of TMC1 fragments interacting with CIB2 and CIB3.
evidence: This claim is supported by AlphaFold 2 modeling predictions and validated by NMR spectroscopy experiments showing simultaneous binding of TMC1-NT and TMC1-IL1 to CIB2 and CIB3.

claim: TMCs are structurally stabilized by CIB proteins to form cation channels.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations of TMC1/2 complexes with CIB2/3 predict that TMCs are structurally stabilized by CIB proteins to form cation channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulations showing that CIB proteins stabilize TMC structures and that TMC1/2 complexes conduct cations.

claim: Intact CIB2/3 and TMC1/2 complexes are integral to hair-cell MET function in vertebrate mechanosensory epithelia.
source: Overall, our work demonstrates that intact CIB2/3 and TMC1/2 complexes are integral to hair-cell MET function in vertebrate mechanosensory epithelia.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined genetic, functional, structural, and computational data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The vertebrate senses of hearing and balance depend on the process of MET in inner-ear hair cells.
source: The vertebrate senses of hearing and balance depend on the process of MET in inner-ear hair cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in the field of auditory and vestibular physiology.

claim: Mechanical forces from sound waves and head movements deflect stereocilia.
source: This process is initiated when mechanical forces from sound waves and head movements deflect specialized mechanosensory projections at the apical surface of hair cells, known as stereocilia (reviewed in Fettiplace, 2017; Frolenkov et al., 2004; Gillespie and Müller, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles in the field.

claim: Deflections of stereocilia result in tensioning of the extracellular tip links that convey mechanical force to the MET channels.
source: Deflections of stereocilia result in tensioning of the extracellular tip links that convey mechanical force to the MET channels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of mechanotransduction in hair cells.

claim: Mature tip links are heterotetrameric filaments composed of cadherin 23 (CDH23) and protocadherin 15 (PCDH15).
source: Mature tip links are heterotetrameric filaments composed of cadherin 23 (CDH23) and protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) (Ahmed et al., 2006; Kazmierczak et al., 2007; Siemens et al., 2004; Söllner et al., 2004; Sotomayor et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In mammalian auditory hair cells, MET channels are localized at the PCDH15 end of the tip link.
source: In mammalian auditory hair cells, MET channels are localized at the PCDH15 end of the tip link (Beurg et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: TMC1 and TMC2 are the pore-forming subunits of the MET channel.
source: Significant progress in our understanding of MET has been recently made by identifying the transmembrane channel-like proteins 1 and 2 (TMC1 and TMC2) as the pore-forming subunits of the MET channel (Kawashima et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LHFPL5 binds to PCDH15 and may regulate force transmission to TMC1 and TMC2.
source: LHFPL5 binds to PCDH15 and may regulate force transmission to TMC1 and TMC2 (Qiu et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TMIE interacts with TMC1/2 and regulates unitary conductance and ion selectivity of the MET channels.
source: TMIE also interacts with TMC1/2 and regulates unitary conductance and ion selectivity of the MET channels (Cunningham et al., 2020; Naz et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MET currents can still be recorded from hair cells lacking LHFPL5 or TMIE.
source: Interestingly, MET currents can still be recorded from hair cells lacking LHFPL5 or TMIE, suggesting that neither are essential for channel function (Fettiplace et al., 2022), yet all are needed for sustained hair-cell transduction and normal hearing.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: LHFPL5 and TMIE are not essential for MET channel function but are needed for sustained hair-cell transduction and normal hearing.
source: Interestingly, MET currents can still be recorded from hair cells lacking LHFPL5 or TMIE, suggesting that neither are essential for channel function (Fettiplace et al., 2022), yet all are needed for sustained hair-cell transduction and normal hearing.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and represents an inference about the functional roles of these proteins.

claim: In zebrafish, Tmcs, Lhfpl5, Tmie, and Pcdh15 are essential for sensory transduction.
source: In zebrafish, Tmcs, Lhfpl5, Tmie, and Pcdh15 are also essential for sensory transduction, suggesting that these molecules form the core MET complex in all vertebrate hair cells (Chen et al., 2020; Erickson et al., 2019; Erickson et al., 2017; Ernest et al., 2000; Gleason et al., 2009; Gopal et al., 2015; Maeda et al., 2017; Maeda et al., 2014; Pacentine and Nicolson, 2019; Phillips et al., 2011; Seiler et al., 2004; Söllner et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research in zebrafish.

claim: Tmcs, Lhfpl5, Tmie, and Pcdh15 form the core MET complex in all vertebrate hair cells.
source: In zebrafish, Tmcs, Lhfpl5, Tmie, and Pcdh15 are also essential for sensory transduction, suggesting that these molecules form the core MET complex in all vertebrate hair cells (Chen et al., 2020; Erickson et al., 2019; Erickson et al., 2017; Ernest et al., 2000; Gleason et al., 2009; Gopal et al., 2015; Maeda et al., 2017; Maeda et al., 2014; Pacentine and Nicolson, 2019; Phillips et al., 2011; Seiler et al., 2004; Söllner et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on zebrafish data cited and represents a generalization to all vertebrates.

claim: CIB2 and CIB3 interact with TMC1/2.
source: We previously showed that calcium (Ca2+) and integrin-binding protein 2 (CIB2), and the closely related CIB3, interact with TMC1/2 (Giese et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: CIB2 is essential for MET function in auditory hair cells.
source: Furthermore, we also demonstrated that CIB2 is essential for MET function in auditory hair cells (Giese et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Recessive variants of CIB2 predominantly cause nonsyndromic DFNB48 hearing loss in humans.
source: Recessive variants of CIB2 predominantly cause nonsyndromic DFNB48 hearing loss in humans (Booth et al., 2018; Michel et al., 2017; Riazuddin et al., 2012; Seco et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Recessive alleles of Cib2 cause hearing loss in mice but no vestibular deficits.
source: Similarly, recessive alleles of Cib2 cause hearing loss in mice but no vestibular deficits (Giese et al., 2017; Michel et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Knockdown of Cib2 in zebrafish diminishes both the acoustic startle response and mechanosensitive responses of lateral-line hair cells.
source: In zebrafish, the knockdown of Cib2 diminishes both the acoustic startle response and mechanosensitive responses of lateral-line hair cells (Riazuddin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CIB2 belongs to a family of four closely related proteins (CIB1-4) that have partial functional redundancy.
source: CIB2 belongs to a family of four closely related proteins (CIB1-4) that have partial functional redundancy and similar structural domains, with at least two Ca2+/Mg2+-binding EF-hand motifs that are highly conserved for CIB2/3 (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CIB proteins have at least two Ca2+/Mg2+-binding EF-hand motifs that are highly conserved for CIB2/3.
source: CIB2 belongs to a family of four closely related proteins (CIB1-4) that have partial functional redundancy and similar structural domains, with at least two Ca2+/Mg2+-binding EF-hand motifs that are highly conserved for CIB2/3 (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Loss of CIB1 protein did not affect auditory function in mice.
source: Wang and co-authors investigated the function of Cib1 in cochlear hair cells through the generation of a knockout strain and concluded that although Cib1 is expressed in the mouse cochlear hair cells, loss of CIB1 protein did not affect auditory function (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CIB2 is essential for the proper localization of TMC1/2 at the tips of auditory hair cell stereocilia.
source: A recent study demonstrated that while CIB2 is essential for the proper localization of TMC1/2 at the tips of auditory hair cell stereocilia, CIB3 can restore MET currents in cochlear hair cells lacking CIB2 (Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CIB3 can restore MET currents in cochlear hair cells lacking CIB2.
source: A recent study demonstrated that while CIB2 is essential for the proper localization of TMC1/2 at the tips of auditory hair cell stereocilia, CIB3 can restore MET currents in cochlear hair cells lacking CIB2 (Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A crystal structure of a TMC1 intracellular linker in complex with CIB3 suggests that CIB2/3 proteins are likely to be auxiliary subunits of hair cell MET channels.
source: The same study reported a crystal structure of a TMC1 intracellular linker in complex with CIB3, which suggests that CIB2/3 proteins are likely to be auxiliary subunits of hair cell MET channels (Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and represents an inference from structural data.

claim: Mice lacking both CIB2 and CIB3 have vestibular deficits.
source: This question was addressed in part by another recent study that reported vestibular deficits in mice lacking both CIB2 and CIB3 (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Vestibular hair cells in Cib2KO/KO mice have MET as assessed via uptake of FM 1-43.
source: In contrast to auditory hair cells, we found that the vestibular hair cells in Cib2KO/KO mice apparently have MET. We assessed MET via uptake of FM 1–43 (Figure 1A), a styryl dye that mostly permeates into hair cells through functional MET channels (Meyers et al., 2003), indicating that there may be another CIB protein playing a functionally redundant role.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and cited methodology.

claim: FM 1-43 is a styryl dye that mostly permeates into hair cells through functional MET channels.
source: We assessed MET via uptake of FM 1–43 (Figure 1A), a styryl dye that mostly permeates into hair cells through functional MET channels (Meyers et al., 2003), indicating that there may be another CIB protein playing a functionally redundant role.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: All four members of the Cib family are expressed in mouse inner ear tissues.
source: Bulk RNA sequencing revealed that all four members of the Cib family are expressed in mouse inner ear tissues (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Only Cib2 and Cib3 are expressed in immature hair cells in the mouse utricle.
source: However, when assessed by single-cell RNA sequencing analysis, only Cib2 and Cib3 are expressed in immature hair cells in the mouse utricle (Figure 1C), a vestibular sensory organ required to detect linear acceleration (McInturff et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mouse utricle is a vestibular sensory organ required to detect linear acceleration.
source: However, when assessed by single-cell RNA sequencing analysis, only Cib2 and Cib3 are expressed in immature hair cells in the mouse utricle (Figure 1C), a vestibular sensory organ required to detect linear acceleration (McInturff et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The expression of Cib2 and Cib3 is maintained in mature type I and type II utricular hair cells.
source: Furthermore, we find that the expression of Cib2 and Cib3 is maintained in mature type I and type II utricular hair cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In immature utricular hair cells, Tmc1 is highly expressed, while Tmc2 expression is low.
source: We also examined the expression of Tmc1 and Tmc2 in utricular hair cells and found that in immature hair cells, Tmc1 is highly expressed, while Tmc2 expression is low (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Tmc2 expression increases during development but remains below Tmc1 levels in both type I and type II hair cells upon maturation.
source: Tmc2 expression increases during development but remains below Tmc1 levels in both type I and type II hair cells upon maturation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CIB2 and CIB3 have been reported to interact with TMC1/2.
source: CIB2 and CIB3 have been reported to interact with TMC1/2, and CIB2 is essential for auditory hair cell MET (Giese et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cib3KO/KO mice have normal hearing at P16.
source: We first characterized hearing function in Cib3KO/KO and control littermate mice at P16 by measuring auditory-evoked brainstem responses (ABRs). Normal ABR waveforms and thresholds were observed in Cib3KO/KO indicating normal hearing.
evidence: This claim is supported by ABR measurement data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice are profoundly deaf.
source: Similar to what has been previously reported in Cib2KO/KO mice (Giese et al., 2017; Michel et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017), the Cib2:Cib3 double knockout (Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO) mice were also profoundly deaf. The Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice did not respond to click or strong tone burst stimuli at 100  dB sound pressure level (SPL) (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ABR measurement data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Auditory hair cells in Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice did not accumulate FM 1-43 dye.
source: As reported previously for Cib2KO/KO mice, we observed that auditory hair cells in Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice did not accumulate FM 1–43 dye (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 dye uptake data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice show progressive degeneration of auditory hair cells.
source: Also, similar to Cib2KO/KO mice (Giese et al., 2017; Michel et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017), we observed progressive degeneration of auditory hair cells in Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D and citations to prior research.

claim: CIB2 is indispensable for hearing and MET function in the auditory hair cells.
source: Taken together with previous studies, our results confirm that CIB2 is indispensable for hearing and MET function in the auditory hair cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data from the current study and prior research.

claim: Cib3KO/KO mice did not display any obvious indications of vestibular dysfunction.
source: Similar to Cib2KO/KO mice (Giese et al., 2017), Cib3KO/KO mice did not display any obvious indications of vestibular dysfunction, such as circling, hyperactivity, or head bobbing, performed well when exploratory behavior was tested, and had normal vestibulo-ocular reflexes (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral and VOR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice showed altered exploratory behavior in an open-field test.
source: In contrast, visual observation of the Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice indicated altered exploratory behavior in an open-field test, suggesting an impairment of the vestibular system (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by open-field test data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice generated negligible eye movements in response to VORd testing.
source: In response to VORd testing, Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice generated robust compensatory eye movements (Figure 3C, black trace). In contrast, Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice generated negligible eye movements (Figure 3C, red trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by VORd testing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: VORd gains in Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice were near zero and significantly reduced compared to Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice.
source: Consistent with this observation, quantification of the VORd across frequencies (Figure 3D) revealed gains near zero in the Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice that were significantly reduced (p<0.05) compared to those measured in Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by VORd gain quantification data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: VORd gains of Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO mice showed attenuation with a significant decrease at 2 Hz compared to Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice.
source: Interestingly, the VORd gains of Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO mice also showed attenuation with a significant decrease at 2 Hz (p<0.01) compared to Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by VORd gain data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The response phase of VORd eye movements was comparable for Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO and Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice at all frequencies.
source: On the other hand, the response phase of VORd eye movements was comparable for Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO and Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice at all frequencies (p>0.05) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by VORd phase data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The VOR is mediated by a direct three-neuron pathway linking the vestibular nerve to the extraocular muscles.
source: The VOR is mediated by a direct three-neuron pathway linking the vestibular nerve to the extraocular muscles and produces compensatory eye movements in the direction opposite of the head movement to provide a stable gaze (reviewed in Cullen, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: OKR responses of Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO and Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO mice were similar.
source: Both Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO and Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO showed robust OKN responses which similarly decreased as a function of frequency (Figure 3E; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by OKR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: OKR gain values in Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice were comparable to controls with the exception of a significant gain decrease at 0.2 Hz.
source: Likewise, OKR gain values in Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO were comparable with the single exception of a significant gain decrease at 0.2 Hz (p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by OKR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice exhibited circling behavior.
source: First, quantification of open-field testing experiments confirmed that mice exhibited circling – a behavior that is commonly associated with loss of vestibular function in mice (Figure 3B; p<0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by open-field testing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice exhibited significantly poorer performance on the rotarod test compared to Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO and Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO mice.
source: While Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO and Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO mice exhibited similar performance, Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice exhibited significantly poorer performance across all time points from day 1 through day 4 (Figure 3G, p<0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by rotarod test data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice commonly displayed head bobbing.
source: Finally, it was also possible to distinguish Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice from the other two groups in their home cages since they commonly displayed head bobbing, a trait also generally associated with vestibular dysfunction in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice showed significantly higher power in head movements in all six dimensions of motion compared to Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO and Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice.
source: Analysis of power spectra of head motion revealed significantly higher power for Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice in all six dimensions of motion, as compared to Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO and Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice (Figure 3H, compare red vs. blue and black).
evidence: This claim is supported by head motion analysis data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: There were no significant differences in the head movements power spectra of Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO and Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice.
source: Furthermore, there were no significant differences in the head movements power spectra of Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO and Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice (Figure 3H, blue vs. black).
evidence: This claim is supported by head motion analysis data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice show marked deficits in vestibulomotor function.
source: Taken together our findings indicate that Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice show marked deficits in vestibulomotor function when compared to both Cib2KO/+;Cib3KO/KO and Cib2+/+;Cib3KO/KO mice.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined vestibular function test data.

claim: High-resolution confocal imaging did not reveal any obvious vestibular hair cell loss in Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice.
source: High-resolution confocal imaging did not reveal any obvious vestibular hair cell loss in Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At P5, FM 1-43 labeling of Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO vestibular tissue failed to label vestibular hair cells in appreciable numbers.
source: At P5, FM 1–43 labeling of Cib2KO/KO; Cib3KO/KO tissue failed to label vestibular hair cells in appreciable numbers (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 labeling data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Fixable FM 1-43 FX intraperitoneal injections at P60 showed no dye uptake in Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO mice.
source: Similarly, fixable FM 1–43 FX intraperitoneal injections at P60 also showed no dye uptake in Cib2KO/KO; Cib3KO/KO mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 FX labeling data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cib2KO/KO and Cib3KO/KO single mutant mice had dye uptake both in striolar and extrastriolar hair cells.
source: Cib2KO/KO and Cib3KO/KO single mutant mice had dye uptake both in striolar and extrastriolar hair cells, although a subtle reduction in FM 1–43 FX was observed in extrastriolar hair cells of both single mutants at P60 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 FX labeling data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CIB2 and CIB3 have compulsory but functionally redundant roles in the vestibular hair cell MET complex.
source: Taken together, these results support compulsory but functionally redundant roles for CIB2 and CIB3 in the vestibular hair cell MET complex.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined genetic and functional data from vestibular hair cells.

claim: The same proteins are required for hair cell MET in zebrafish and mammals.
source: Numerous studies have shown that the same proteins are required for hair cell MET in zebrafish and mammals (Chen et al., 2020; Erickson et al., 2017; Ernest et al., 2000; Gleason et al., 2009; Gopal et al., 2015; Maeda et al., 2017; Maeda et al., 2014; Phillips et al., 2011; Seiler et al., 2004; Söllner et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Zebrafish rely on their saccule for hearing and utricle for balance.
source: Unlike mammals, the zebrafish's inner ear does not have a cochlea. Instead, zebrafish rely on their saccule for hearing and utricle for balance.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish anatomy and physiology.

claim: Zebrafish utilize hair cells in the lateral line to detect local water movement.
source: Zebrafish also utilize hair cells in a specialized sensory system, the lateral line, to detect local water movement.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish sensory systems.

claim: Hair cells within both the zebrafish inner ear and lateral line share many morphological similarities to mammalian vestibular hair cells.
source: The hair cells within both the zebrafish inner ear and lateral line share many morphological similarities to mammalian vestibular hair cells (Nicolson, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Zebrafish scRNAseq data show that both cib2 and cib3 are expressed in the inner ear while primarily cib2 is expressed in lateral-line hair cells.
source: Zebrafish scRNAseq data show that both cib2 and cib3 are expressed in the inner ear while primarily cib2 is expressed in lateral-line hair cells (Baek et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior scRNAseq studies.

claim: The probability of a startle response was significantly reduced in cib2 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
source: We found that, compared to controls, the probability of a startle response was significantly reduced in cib2 mutants (Figure 5A, control: 0.71 ± 0.04; cib2: 0.28 ± 0.06, p=0.005).
evidence: This claim is supported by acoustic startle response data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: cib3 mutant zebrafish startle with a similar frequency compared to controls.
source: In contrast, cib3 mutants startle with a similar frequency compared to controls (Figure 5A, p=0.36).
evidence: This claim is supported by acoustic startle response data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: cib2;cib3 mutant zebrafish exhibited a complete absence of startle responses.
source: In cib2;cib3 mutant animals we observed a complete absence of startle responses (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by acoustic startle response data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: cib2;cib3 mutant zebrafish exhibited spontaneous circling behavior.
source: Furthermore, we observed that cib2;cib3 mutants but not cib2 or cib3 mutants exhibited spontaneous circling behavior, an additional indicator of inner ear dysfunction in zebrafish (Nicolson et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data and a citation to prior research.

claim: Cib2 and Cib3 are both required to ensure normal acoustic startle responses in zebrafish.
source: Together our behavioral results indicate that Cib2 and Cib3 are both required to ensure normal acoustic startle responses in zebrafish.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined acoustic startle response data from zebrafish mutants.

claim: Loss of Cib2, but not Cib3, can impair auditory function in zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, just loss of Cib2, but not Cib3 can impair auditory function in zebrafish.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the acoustic startle response data showing reduced responses in cib2 mutants but not cib3 mutants.

claim: The percent of hair cells per neuromast labeling with FM 1-43 was significantly reduced in cib2 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
source: We found that, compared to controls, the percent of hair cells per neuromast labeling with FM 1–43 was significantly reduced in cib2 mutants (Figure 5B, D and E, control: 97.6 ± 1.2; cib2: 37.5 ± 6.9, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 labeling data shown in Figure 5B, D, and E.

claim: A similar percent of hair cells per neuromast labeled with FM 1-43 in cib3 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
source: In contrast, a similar percent of hair cells per neuromast labeled with FM 1–43 in cib3 mutants, compared to controls (Figure 5B, D and F, cib3: 95.7 ± 1.9, p=1.0).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 labeling data shown in Figure 5B, D, and F.

claim: The average FM 1-43 label was reduced in cib2 but not cib3 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
source: We found that, compared to controls, the average FM 1–43 label was reduced in cib2 but not cib3 mutants (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 intensity quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In cib2;cib3 mutant zebrafish, there was a complete absence of FM 1-43 labeling in lateral-line hair cells.
source: In cib2;cib3 mutant animals we observed a complete absence of FM 1–43 labeling in lateral-line hair cells (Figure 5B, D and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 labeling data shown in Figure 5B, D, and G.

claim: Both Cib2 and Cib3 are needed to ensure normal MET in all lateral-line hair cells in zebrafish.
source: Thus, taken together the results of our FM 1–43 labeling analysis are consistent with a requirement for both Cib2 and Cib3 to ensure normal MET in all lateral-line hair cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined FM 1-43 labeling data from zebrafish mutants.

claim: Significantly fewer cells were mechanosensitive in cib2 and cib2;cib3 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
source: We quantified the number of hair bundles per neuromast with mechanosensitive Ca2+ responses, and found that compared to controls, significantly fewer cells were mechanosensitive in cib2 and cib2;cib3 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, control: 92.2 ± 2.5; cib2: 49.9 ± 5.8, cib2;cib3: 19.0 ± 6.6, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In cib3 mutant zebrafish, the percent of mechanosensitive cells per neuromast was similar compared to controls.
source: In contrast, in cib3 mutants, the percent of mechanosensitive cells per neuromast was similar compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, cib3: 94.5 ± 1.8, p=1.0).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The magnitude of mechanosensitive Ca2+ responses in cib2 and cib2;cib3 hair bundles were significantly reduced compared to controls.
source: This quantification revealed that, while cib3 mechanosensitive responses were not different compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C, GCaMP6s % ∆F/F control: 70.6±5.9; cib3: 71.6±5.2, p>1.0), the magnitude of responses in cib2 and cib2;cib3 hair bundles were significantly reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C, GCaMP6s % ∆F/F control: 70.6 ± 5.9; cib2: 33.0 ± 5.8, cib2;cib3: 14.7 ± 1.9, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: Loss of Cib2 alone, but not Cib3, can impair mechanosensory function in the majority of zebrafish lateral-line hair cells.
source: Overall, our in vivo FM 1–43 and Ca2+-imaging analyses revealed that loss of Cib2 alone, but not Cib3 can impair mechanosensory function in the majority of zebrafish lateral-line hair cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined FM 1-43 and calcium imaging data from zebrafish mutants.

claim: Cib2 and Cib3 are both required to ensure normal MET function in all lateral-line hair cells in zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, Cib2 and Cib3 are both required to ensure normal MET function in all lateral-line hair cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined functional data from zebrafish mutants.

claim: In the zebrafish pLL, hair cells that detect posterior flow rely on Tmc2b, while hair cells that detect anterior flow rely on both Tmc2b and Tmc2a.
source: In the primary posterior lateral line (pLL) hair cells are oriented to respond to either anterior or posterior fluid flow. The subset of hair cells that detects posterior flow relies on Tmc2b while the subset that detects anterior flow relies on both Tmc2b and Tmc2a (Figure 6A; Chou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: In the zebrafish crista, short cells rely on Tmc2a, while tall cells rely on either Tmc1 or Tmc2b for mechanosensitive function.
source: Short cells rely on Tmc2a, while tall cells rely on either Tmc1 or Tmc2b for mechanosensitive function (Figure 6E; Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and illustrated in Figure 6E.

claim: In cib2 mutant zebrafish, significantly more of the FM 1-43 positive hair cells in the pLL were oriented to respond to posterior flow.
source: In contrast, when we examined cib2 mutants, we found that significantly more of the FM 1–43 positive hair cells were oriented to respond to posterior flow (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 FX labeling and hair bundle orientation analysis shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: In cib2 mutant zebrafish, the residual Cib3 present in pLL hair cells preferentially functions in hair cells that express primarily Tmc2b and are oriented to respond to posterior flow.
source: This indicates that in cib2 mutants, the residual Cib3 present in pLL hair cells preferentially functions in hair cells that express primarily Tmc2b and are oriented to respond to posterior flow (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the hair cell orientation data in cib2 mutants and known Tmc expression patterns.

claim: Cib2 can function with hair cells that express Tmc2b as well as hair cells that express Tmc2b and Tmc2a.
source: On the other hand, Cib2 can function with hair cells that express Tmc2b (respond to posterior flow) as well as hair cells that express Tmc2b and Tmc2a (respond to anterior flow).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the hair cell orientation data in cib2 mutants and known Tmc expression patterns.

claim: No hair cells in the medial cristae were FM 4-64 positive in cib2;cib3 double mutant zebrafish.
source: We found that similar to our FM 1–43 results in the pLL, no hair cells in the medial cristae were FM 4–64 positive in cib2;cib3 double mutants (Figure 6I–I').
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 4-64 labeling data shown in Figure 6I-I'.

claim: There were no defects in FM 4-64 labeling in the crista of cib3 mutant zebrafish compared to controls.
source: In addition, similar to the pLL we observed no defects in FM 4–64 labeling in the crista of cib3 mutants compared to controls (Figure 6G–G').
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 4-64 labeling data shown in Figure 6G-G'.

claim: Short hair cells in the crista of cib2 mutant zebrafish failed to label with FM 4-64.
source: Interestingly we found that short hair cells in the crista of cib2 mutants failed to label with FM 4–64 (Figure 6H–H').
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 4-64 labeling data shown in Figure 6H-H'.

claim: Cib2 is required for mechanosensitive function in hair cells that express Tmc2a in zebrafish.
source: Overall, our functional assessment of MET based on hair cell subtypes within the zebrafish pLL and inner ear suggests that Cib2 is required for mechanosensitive function in hair cells that express Tmc2a.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined functional data from different hair cell subtypes in zebrafish.

claim: The AF2 model of TMC1 alone resembles previous TMEM16/OSCA-based models of TMC1.
source: The AF2 model of TMC1 alone resembles previous TMEM16/OSCA-based models of TMC1 and is also consistent with a recent cryo-EM structure of the worm TMC-1 protein (Ballesteros et al., 2018; Jeong et al., 2022; Pan et al., 2018; Walujkar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural studies and represents a comparison of models.

claim: TMC1 has ten transmembrane domains (α1 to α10).
source: In these models, TMC1 has ten transmembrane domains (α1 to α10; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—source data 1) and a putative pore is formed by transmembrane helices α4, α5, α6, and α7 at the periphery of each monomer (Pan et al., 2018; Walujkar et al., 2021), away from the dimeric interface involving α10.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior research.

claim: A putative pore in TMC1 is formed by transmembrane helices α4, α5, α6, and α7 at the periphery of each monomer.
source: In these models, TMC1 has ten transmembrane domains (α1 to α10; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—source data 1) and a putative pore is formed by transmembrane helices α4, α5, α6, and α7 at the periphery of each monomer (Pan et al., 2018; Walujkar et al., 2021), away from the dimeric interface involving α10.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling data and citations to prior research.

claim: AF2 models of TMC1 feature an additional amphipathic helix, denoted α0, extending almost parallel to the expected plane of the membrane bilayer.
source: Our new models feature an additional amphipathic helix, which we denote α0, extending almost parallel to the expected plane of the membrane bilayer without crossing towards the extracellular side (as observed for a mostly hydrophobic α0 in OSCA channels and labeled as H3 in the worm TMC-1 structure) (Jeong et al., 2022; Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling data and citations to prior research.

claim: The intracellular domain linking helices α2 and α3 (IL1) adopts a helix-loop-helix fold.
source: The intracellular domain linking helices α2 and α3, denoted here as IL1, adopts a helix-loop-helix with the two helices running parallel to each other and differing in length (Figure 7—figure supplements 1–4; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 1-4.

claim: The IL1 fold is the same as observed in its crystal structure in complex with CIB3.
source: This is the same fold observed in its crystal structure in complex with CIB3 (Liang et al., 2021), which validated the modeling approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior structural research and validates the modeling approach.

claim: AF2 models of TMC1 in complex with CIB2 suggest that the N-terminus (NT) of TMC1 also interacts with CIB2.
source: Interestingly, AF2 models of TMC1 in complex with CIB2 suggest that the N-terminus (NT) of TMC1 also interacts with CIB2 (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by AF2 modeling data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: In the AF2 model, CIB2 is clamped between TMC1-NT and TMC1-IL1.
source: In our model, CIB2 is clamped between TMC1-NT and TMC1-IL1 while the first helix of TMC1-IL1 runs parallel to the membrane plane interacting with the base of α1 and the intracellular linkers between α4 and α5, α6 and α7, and α8 and α9.
evidence: This claim is supported by AF2 modeling data and structural analysis.

claim: The predicted interaction between TMC1-NT and CIB2 is consistent with previous biochemical data.
source: Notably, the predicted interaction between TMC1-NT and CIB2 is consistent with previous biochemical data (Giese et al., 2017), while the overall model resolves seemingly contradictory results indicating that either the NT or IL1 of TMC1 was responsible for interactions with CIB proteins (Giese et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies and represents a reconciliation of previous findings.

claim: AF2 models of TMC1 with CIB3 and of TMC2 with CIB2/3 predicted the same architecture for the TMC1/2 + CIB2/3 complexes where CIB proteins are clamped between the IL1 and NT domains of TMCs.
source: Additional AF2 models of TMC1 with CIB3 and of TMC2 with CIB2/3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) predicted the same architecture for the TMC1/2 + CIB2/3 complexes where CIB proteins are clamped between the IL1 and NT domains of TMCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by AF2 modeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Predictions for fish TMC + CIB complexes show the same general architecture as mammalian complexes.
source: Predictions for fish complexes also show the same general architecture (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by AF2 modeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NMR experiments validated the clamp model for Homo sapiens TMC + CIB interactions.
source: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) experiments were used to validate the clamp model for Homo sapiens (hs) TMC + CIB interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The addition of hs TMC1-NT induced additional chemical shift perturbations in [U-15N]-hs CIB2 + hs TMC1-IL1, demonstrating that TMC1-IL1 and TMC1-NT bind simultaneously to CIB2.
source: Moreover, the addition of hs TMC1-NT induced additional chemical shift perturbations in many, but not all peaks, demonstrating that the TMC1-IL1 and TMC1-NT ligands bind simultaneously to [U-15N]-hs CIB2 (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 6B.

claim: Similar NMR results were observed for [U-15N]-hs CIB3 with TMC1-IL1 and TMC1-NT.
source: We observed similar results when comparing spectra for [U-15N]-hs CIB3 alone, co-refolded with hs TMC1-IL1, and upon addition of hs TMC1-NT (Figure 7—figure supplement 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6C-D.

claim: Direct heteromeric interactions between CIB2 and CIB3 are unlikely.
source: A control experiment with the co-refolded mix of hs CIB3 + hs TMC1-IL1 and [U-15N]-hs CIB2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 6E) revealed no change in chemical shifts indicating that direct heteromeric interactions between CIB2 and CIB3 are unlikely.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR control experiment data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6E.

claim: NMR data strongly support a model in which human CIB2/3 proteins are clamped between TMC1-IL1 and TMC1-NT.
source: Thus, taken together, the NMR data strongly support a model in which human CIB2/3 proteins are clamped between TMC1-IL1 and TMC1-NT as suggested by AF2 and consistent with prior biochemical data revealing interactions with either TMC1-NT or TMC1-IL1 (Giese et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined NMR data, AF2 modeling, and prior biochemical studies.

claim: Equilibrium simulations of TMC1 and TMC2 alone revealed stable conformations for the transmembrane domains but a highly mobile NT domain.
source: Equilibrium simulations of TMC1 and TMC2 alone revealed stable conformations for the transmembrane domains of these proteins, but a highly mobile NT domain (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: In simulations where CIB2 or CIB3 were present, more stable conformations of N-termini along with stable salt bridges were observed.
source: In simulations where CIB2 or CIB3 were present, with or without bound Ca2+, we observed more stable conformations of N-termini along with stable salt bridges (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: BSA analysis suggests that TMC1 and TMC2 have more contacts with CIB3 than with CIB2.
source: Buried surface area (BSA) for the TMC + CIB complexes (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A, C and E, Figure 8—source data 2) revealed a possible trend in which TMC1 and TMC2 have more contacts with CIB3 than with CIB2.
evidence: This claim is supported by BSA analysis from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Parts of the amphipathic α0 helices spontaneously partitioned at the membrane interface with their hydrophobic sides pointing toward the lipid bilayer core.
source: Longer, Anton 2, 960-ns long equilibrium trajectories of TMC1 with CIB2 and bound Ca2+ in a mixed bilayer and TMC1 with CIB2 and (un)bound Ca2+ in a POPC bilayer revealed how parts of the amphipathic α0 helices spontaneously partitioned at the membrane interface with their hydrophobic sides pointing toward the lipid bilayer core (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Anton 2 simulation data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The N-terminal cytoplasmic domain of LHFPL5 has been shown to interact with the TMC1 amphipathic helix, which might be essential for channel function in mice.
source: The N-terminal cytoplasmic domain of LHFPL5 has been shown to interact with this TMC1 amphipathic helix, which might be essential for channel function in mice (Qiu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In Anton 2 equilibrium trajectories, contacts between CIB2 and the TMC1-IL1 and -NT remained, confirming the stability of the complex over a microsecond timescale.
source: Regardless, in all Anton 2 equilibrium trajectories contacts between CIB2 and the TMC1-IL1 and -NT remained, thus confirming the stability of the complex over a microsecond timescale.
evidence: This claim is supported by Anton 2 simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In systems with pure POPC bilayers, permeation of K+ was observed in either one or both pores of the TMC1 dimer, with or without CIB2 or CIB3 and with or without bound Ca2+.
source: In systems with pure POPC bilayers, we observed permeation of K+ in either one or both pores of the TMC1 dimer, with or without CIB2 or CIB3 and with or without bound Ca2+, despite the presence of Cl- (150 mM KCl).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data with applied voltage.

claim: In all cases where a clear conductive state was monitored, almost exclusive passage of K+ was observed with conductance values that reached up to ~138 pS for a single pore.
source: Variability of the conductance state was attributed to partial blockage by lipids and poor sampling, but in all cases in which a clear conductive state was monitored, we observed the almost exclusive passage of K+ with conductance values that reached up to ~138 pS for a single pore.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data with applied voltage.

claim: The conductance values monitored in simulations are consistent with previous simulations and with the expected conductance of the inner-ear transduction channel.
source: While simulations tend to overestimate bulk KCl conductivity and in some cases, predictions need to be scaled down (by a factor of ~0.6) (Walujkar et al., 2021), the conductance values monitored here are consistent with previous simulations and with the expected conductance of the inner-ear transduction channel (Beurg et al., 2021; Walujkar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to prior simulation and experimental data.

claim: Smaller conductance values were observed for TMC1 systems with mixed lipid bilayers compared to POPC bilayers.
source: In contrast, we observed smaller conductance values for TMC1 systems with mixed lipid bilayers (at most ~22 pS for a single pore), regardless of the presence of CIB2 or CIB3, with or without bound Ca2+ (Figure 8—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The reduced conductance values observed for mixed-membrane systems were attributed in part to pore blockage by cholesterol and lipids in the initial setup.
source: The reduced conductance values observed for mixed-membrane systems were attributed in part to pore blockage by cholesterol and lipids in the initial setup.
evidence: This is an inference based on analysis of the simulation trajectories.

claim: Anton 2 simulations revealed a trend in which TMC1 exhibits higher conductance with CIB2 bound.
source: Interestingly, Anton 2 simulations of TMC1, TMC1 + CIB2, and TMC1 + CIB2 + Ca2+ in pure POPC membranes subjected to –0.5 V, –0.25 V, and –0.125 V for 480 ns, 480 ns, and 960 ns, respectively, revealed a trend in which TMC1 exhibits higher conductance with CIB2 bound (Figure 8E, Figure 8—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Anton 2 simulation data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The observation that TMC1 exhibits higher conductance with CIB2 bound may explain why CIB2 is essential for normal TMC1 function.
source: This may begin to explain why CIB2 is essential for normal TMC1 function.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the simulation data showing increased conductance with CIB2.

claim: Simulations of TMC2 with an applied transmembrane voltage revealed a more closed state when compared to TMC1.
source: Simulations of TMC2 with an applied transmembrane voltage of –0.5 V revealed a more closed state when compared to our TMC1 model, regardless of membrane composition and presence or absence of CIB2, CIB3, and bound Ca2+ (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: The maximum conductance for TMC2 did not reach above ~64 pS, suggesting that the conformation simulated is less open than the ones explored in simulations of TMC1.
source: Conduction of K+ was observed in most cases, but the maximum conductance did not reach above ~64 pS, suggesting that the conformation simulated is less open than the ones explored in simulations of TMC1.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the conductance values observed in TMC2 simulations.

claim: TMC2 may have an intrinsic lower single-channel conductance than TMC1.
source: We also speculate that this is due to TMC2 having an intrinsic lower single-channel conductance than TMC1, as has been suggested by some experiments (Kim et al., 2013), but not others (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on simulation data and conflicting prior experimental results.

claim: The TMC2 model may not be in a fully open conformation, which can only be reached upon mechanical stimulation.
source: It is also possible that our TMC2 model is not in a fully open conformation, which can only be reached upon mechanical stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the limitations of the TMC2 model.

claim: Simulations unequivocally indicate that TMC1 and TMC2 are cation channels.
source: Regardless, our simulations unequivocally indicate that TMC1 and TMC2 are cation channels and that these proteins can form stable complexes with CIB2 and CIB3.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined molecular dynamics simulation data showing K+ permeation.

claim: TMC1 and TMC2 can form stable complexes with CIB2 and CIB3.
source: Regardless, our simulations unequivocally indicate that TMC1 and TMC2 are cation channels and that these proteins can form stable complexes with CIB2 and CIB3.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined molecular dynamics simulation data showing stable interactions.

claim: CIB2 and CIB3 are important for stereocilia maintenance and MET in mouse vestibular hair cells.
source: Recently, Wang et al., 2023 have suggested that CIB2 and CIB3 are important for stereocilia maintenance and MET in mouse vestibular hair cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Cib2 is highly expressed in the striolar region while Cib3 is expressed in the extrastriolar regions of mouse vestibular organs.
source: This work demonstrated that similar to Tmc1 and Tmc2, Cib2 is highly expressed in the striolar region while Cib3 is expressed in the extrastriolar regions, and mice lacking both Cib2 and Cib3 had no MET and deficits in vestibular hair cell bundle structure (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Vestibular hair cells in mice and zebrafish lacking CIB2 and CIB3 are not degenerated but have no detectable MET.
source: We demonstrate that vestibular hair cells in mice and zebrafish lacking CIB2 and CIB3 are not degenerated but have no detectable MET, assessed via FM 1–43 dye uptake, at time points when MET function is well developed in wild-type hair cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the current study.

claim: A similar structural-function phenotype has been reported in auditory hair cells in Tmc1/Tmc2 double mutant mice.
source: Similar structural-function phenotype has been reported in auditory hair cells in Tmc1/Tmc2 double mutant mice (Kawashima et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The study provides strong genetic evidence for the direct functional relationship between CIB and TMC proteins in regulating MET both in auditory and vestibular hair cells.
source: Besides the known in vitro interactions (Giese et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2021), our study provides strong genetic evidence for the direct functional relationship between CIB and TMC proteins in regulating MET both in auditory and vestibular hair cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined genetic and functional data from the current study.

claim: The loss of CIB2 leads to profound hearing loss from birth in both humans and mice.
source: Previous studies have shown that the loss of CIB2 leads to profound hearing loss from birth in both humans and mice (Giese et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2021; Seco et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The endogenous levels of CIB3 present in auditory hair cells are not sufficient to compensate for CIB2 in hearing.
source: This suggests that the endogenous levels of CIB3 present in auditory hair cells are not sufficient to compensate for CIB2 in hearing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that loss of CIB2 causes hearing loss despite CIB3 expression.

claim: Over-expression of CIB3 in mouse auditory outer hair cells can only partially compensate for the loss of CIB2 in MET.
source: Prior work has also shown that over-expression of CIB3 in mouse auditory outer hair cells can only partially compensate for the loss of CIB2 in MET (Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Compared to auditory hair cells, the expression of CIB3 is several folds higher in vestibular end organs.
source: While CIB2 is also present in vestibular hair cells, compared to auditory hair cells, the expression of CIB3 is several folds higher in vestibular end organs.
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Endogenous levels of CIB3 can fully compensate for the loss of CIB2 in vestibular hair cells in mice.
source: Indeed, our current data demonstrate that, unlike auditory hair cells, endogenous levels of CIB3 can fully compensate for the loss of CIB2 in vestibular hair cells in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data from vestibular hair cells in the current study.

claim: Both CIB2 and CIB3 can play overlapping roles in MET function in the vestibular system in mice.
source: Together our work on the vestibular system in mice highlights that both CIB2 and CIB3 can play overlapping roles in MET function.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data from the vestibular system in mice.

claim: In zebrafish, Cib3 can compensate for Cib2, but only in specific subsets of hair cells.
source: Interestingly, our corresponding work in zebrafish indicates that Cib3 can also compensate for Cib2, but only in specific subsets of hair cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data from zebrafish hair cells in the current study.

claim: In the zebrafish crista, short cells rely on Tmc2a while tall cells rely on Tmc2b and Tmc1.
source: Genetic studies have revealed that these two types of hair cells rely on different Tmc combinations for MET–short cells rely on Tmc2a while tall cells rely on Tmc2b and Tmc1 (Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cib2 is required in both short and tall cells in the zebrafish crista, while Cib3 is required in just tall cells.
source: Our work on MET in the zebrafish cristae indicates that Cib2 is required in both short and tall cells, while Cib3 is required in just tall cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data from zebrafish crista in the current study.

claim: The loss of Cib3 alone does not impact FM 4-64 labeling in the zebrafish crista, indicating that Cib2 can compensate for the loss of Cib3 in both short and tall cells.
source: In contrast, the loss of Cib3 alone does not impact FM 4–64 labeling in the zebrafish crista, indicating that Cib2 can compensate for the loss of Cib3 in both short and tall cells (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 4-64 labeling data shown in Figure 6G and represents an inference.

claim: Zebrafish cib2 mutants have a severely diminished acoustic startle response.
source: Currently, it is not clear what role different types of hair cells play in zebrafish inner ear epithelia. Our present findings show that zebrafish cib2 mutants have a severely diminished acoustic startle response, a behavior mediated primarily by the saccule (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by acoustic startle response data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cib2 plays an important role in hair cells that detect acoustic stimuli in zebrafish.
source: These behavioral results suggest that Cib2 plays an important role in hair cells that detect acoustic stimuli.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the acoustic startle response data.

claim: In the zebrafish lateral line, cells that detect anterior flow primarily rely on Cib2 for MET.
source: In our work, we find that cells that detect anterior flow primarily rely on Cib2 for MET (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM 1-43 FX labeling and hair bundle orientation data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Cib3 cannot compensate for the loss of Cib2 in zebrafish lateral-line cells that detect anterior flow.
source: Furthermore, this work indicates that Cib3 cannot compensate for the loss of Cib2 in these cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that anterior flow-responsive cells lack FM 1-43 labeling in cib2 mutants.

claim: The functional assessment in the zebrafish lateral line and crista suggests that Cib2 is specifically required for mechanosensitive function in populations of hair cells that express Tmc2a.
source: Interestingly, our functional assessment in the zebrafish lateral line and crista suggests that Cib2 is specifically required for mechanosensitive function in populations of hair cells that express Tmc2a.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined functional data from zebrafish lateral line and crista.

claim: The addition of Tmc2a to lateral-line cells that detect anterior flow significantly augments the mechanosensitive responses of these cells.
source: Recent work has shown that the addition of Tmc2a to lateral-line cells that detect anterior flow significantly augments the mechanosensitive responses of these cells (Kindig et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: In vivo studies of mouse TMC + CIB and zebrafish Tmc + Cib complexes suggest a conserved functional relationship between these two protein families across vertebrates.
source: Our in vivo studies of mouse TMC + CIB and zebrafish Tmc + Cib complexes suggest a conserved functional relationship between these two protein families across vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data from mouse and zebrafish studies.

claim: Structural predictions using AF2 show conserved folds for human and zebrafish TMC and CIB proteins, as well as conserved architecture for their protein complexes.
source: Structural predictions using AF2 show conserved folds for human and zebrafish proteins, as well as conserved architecture for their protein complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by AF2 modeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AF2 predictions are consistent with previous experimentally validated models for the TMC1 pore.
source: Predictions are consistent with previous experimentally validated models for the TMC1 pore (Ballesteros et al., 2018; Pan et al., 2018), with the structure of human CIB3 coupled to mouse TMC1-IL1 (Liang et al., 2021), and with our NMR data validating the interaction between human TMC1 and CIB2/3 proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to prior structural studies and NMR data.

claim: The AF2 models are consistent with the architecture of the nematode TMC-1 and CALM-1 complex, despite low sequence identity.
source: Remarkably, the AF2 models are also consistent with the architecture of the nematode TMC-1 and CALM-1 complex (Jeong et al., 2022), despite low sequence identity (36% between human TMC1 and worm TMC-1 and 51% between human CIB2 and worm CALM-1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to the nematode structure and represents an inference about conservation.

claim: The TMC + CIB functional relationship extends beyond vertebrates.
source: This suggests that the TMC + CIB functional relationship extends beyond vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the structural similarity to nematode proteins.

claim: The modeling predictions, NMR experiments, and simulations provide a structural framework to interpret and understand seemingly contradictory results about TMC-CIB interactions.
source: Taken together, the modeling predictions, NMR experiments, and simulations presented here provide a structural framework to interpret and understand seemingly contradictory results.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined structural and experimental data.

claim: The behavior of CIB2 and CIB3 in solution is different in the absence of TMC1-IL1.
source: Interestingly, the behavior of CIB2 and CIB3 in solution (SEC experiments using 3 mM CaCl2) is different in the absence of TMC1-IL1.
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CIB2 appears as a single peak in SEC experiments, while CIB3 shows two clear peaks indicating the presence of monomeric and dimeric states.
source: While CIB2 appears as a single peak, CIB3 shows two clear peaks indicating the presence of monomeric and dimeric states, consistent with the crystal structure of an apparent CIB3 dimer (Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC data and a citation to prior structural research.

claim: In the presence of TMC1-IL1, the CIB3 dimeric peak is absent.
source: In the presence of TMC1-IL1, the CIB3 dimeric peak is absent, and the potentially monomeric peak is slightly shifted accounting for the added TMC1-IL1, as observed for CIB2.
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CIB2, both in the presence and in the absence of TMC1-IL1, is monomeric in solution.
source: This result suggests that CIB2, both in the presence and in the absence of TMC1-IL1, is monomeric in solution (Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on SEC data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: The proposal that CIB2 is a monomer is consistent with prior conclusions.
source: This proposal is consistent with prior conclusions that CIB2 is a monomer (Dal Cortivo et al., 2019), but is in disagreement with other reports indicating that CIB2 is a dimer in solution (Vallone et al., 2018) and our own prior pull-down assays indicating that CIB2 co-immunoprecipitated with differentially tagged CIB2 or CIB3 (Giese et al., 2017; Riazuddin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and represents a comparison of findings.

claim: The simplest explanation for seemingly contradictory results about CIB oligomerization comes from the TMC1 and TMC2 dimeric states.
source: The simplest explanation for these seemingly contradictory results comes from the TMC1 and TMC2 dimeric states (Pan et al., 2018) and our modeling indicating that each TMC monomer interacts with one CIB protein (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on modeling data and prior research on TMC oligomerization.

claim: Pull-down assays might be reflecting the oligomeric state of TMC proteins rather than direct CIB-CIB interactions.
source: Pull-down assays might simply be reflecting the oligomeric state of TMC proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative inference to explain prior pull-down assay results.

claim: TMC proteins have been suggested to form hetero-oligomers.
source: In such a scenario, and considering that TMC proteins have been suggested to form hetero-oligomers (Pan et al., 2018), there are up to ten different combinations of TMC1/2 and CIB2/3 proteins (Figure 8—figure supplement 5) that might have distinct properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

evidence: This claim is an inference based on the possible combinations of TMC and CIB proteins.

claim: Such variety of TMC/CIB complexes with potentially different conductance values might explain tonotopic changes of conductance along the cochlea.
source: Such variety of complexes with potentially different conductance values might explain tonotopic changes of conductance along the cochlea, although other explanations exist, including a variable number of TMC proteins around the tip link (Beurg et al., 2018) and the direct influence of membrane composition on conductance (Effertz et al., 2017; Walujkar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about possible explanations for tonotopic variation, with citations to alternative explanations.

claim: How TMC + CIB interactions depend on Ca2+ concentration may have important functional implications for adaptation and hair cell mechanotransduction.

claim: Structures of CIB3 and worm CALM-1 both bind divalent ions via EF-hand motifs proximal to their C-termini.
source: Structures of CIB3 and worm CALM-1, a CIB2 homologue, both bind divalent ions via EF-hand motifs proximal to their C-termini (Jeong et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Reports on CIB2 affinities for Ca2+ are inconsistent, with KD values that range from 14 µM to 0.5 mM.
source: Reports on CIB2 affinities for Ca2+ are inconsistent, with KD values that range from 14 µM to 0.5 mM (Blazejczyk et al., 2009; Vallone et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research showing variable results.

claim: Qualitative pull-down assays suggest that the TMC1 and CIB2 interactions are Ca2+-independent.
source: Although qualitative pull-down assays done in the presence or the absence of 5 mM CaCl2 suggest that the TMC1 and CIB2 interactions are Ca2+-independent (Liang et al., 2021), strength and details of the CIB + TMC-IL1 and CIB + TMC-NT contacts might be Ca2+-dependent, especially considering that Ca2+ induces changes that lead to exposure of hydrophobic residues involved in binding (Blazejczyk et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and represents a speculation about Ca2+-dependence.

claim: Simulations in the presence of a biasing potential demonstrate that both TMC1 and TMC2 are cation channels with predicted single-channel conductance values consistent with those of the transduction channel.
source: Our simulations in the presence of a biasing potential unequivocally demonstrate that both TMC1 and TMC2, in the presence or the absence of CIB proteins, with or without bound Ca2+, and in two types of membranes, are cation channels with predicted single-channel conductance values that can reach values that are consistent with those of the transduction channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data with applied voltage.

claim: The models emphasize the role played by the membrane in lining the pore of TMC proteins.
source: Our models emphasize again the role played by the membrane in lining the pore of TMC proteins (Pan et al., 2018; Walujkar et al., 2021), and also indicate that CIB proteins are ideally positioned to connect various parts of cytosolic inter-helix linkers with the helices that form the pore, especially α3 and α4, recently implicated in gating (Akyuz et al., 2022; Walujkar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling and simulation data and citations to prior research.

claim: CIB proteins are ideally positioned to connect various parts of cytosolic inter-helix linkers with the helices that form the pore.

evidence: This claim is an inference based on modeling and simulation data.

claim: The modeling positions the myristoylated N-terminus of CIB2 and CIB3 close enough to the membrane bilayer, which might be another way to sense membrane stretch and influence gating.
source: Last, our modeling also positions the myristoylated N-terminus of CIB2 and CIB3 close enough to the membrane bilayer, which might be yet another way to sense membrane stretch and influence gating.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on modeling data about a potential mechanism.

claim: The biochemically supported atomic-resolution structural models and simulations along with results from animal models strongly suggest that TMC1/2 proteins must function with CIB2/3 in normal hair-cell MET across sensory organs, hair-cell types, and species.
source: Overall, the biochemically supported atomic-resolution structural models and simulations presented here along with our results obtained using animal models strongly suggest that TMC1/2 proteins must function with CIB2/3 in normal hair-cell MET across sensory organs, hair-cell types, and species.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined structural, computational, and in vivo data.

claim: Structural data indicate multiple contact points between TMC and CIB proteins.
source: This is supported by structural data indicating multiple contact points between TMC and CIB proteins, simulation data predicting that CIB proteins stabilize TMC cytosolic domains and may enhance cation conduction, and in vitro and in vivo functional data indicating that both TMC1/2 and CIB2/3 proteins are needed for hair-cell MET.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling and NMR data presented in the manuscript.

evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In vitro and in vivo functional data indicate that both TMC1/2 and CIB2/3 proteins are needed for hair-cell MET.
source: This is supported by structural data indicating multiple contact points between TMC and CIB proteins, simulation data predicting that CIB proteins stabilize TMC cytosolic domains and may enhance cation conduction, and in vitro and in vivo functional data indicating that both TMC1/2 and CIB2/3 proteins are needed for hair-cell MET.
